claim: Human experts at every level revisit the same move at greater depth (progressive deepening). De Groot's 49 protocols averaged about 4 re-investigations per protocol, about equal to the number of different moves tried (n0 4.5). Only 2 protocols had none. Gobet's 48 Swiss players showed the same macro-structure, with no reliable difference from de Groot's sample on any pooled variable.
agent_test: Compare a loop that may re-enter an already-explored candidate with a bigger depth budget against a loop that only expands new candidates, same total tokens, on hard puzzles with verifiable answers.

claim: Which kind of return changes with skill is contested. Gobet (n=48) found stronger players make more immediate returns and fewer non-immediate ones (max NIR F(3,44)=3.71, p<.02; Masters differ only from Class A). De Groot saw two weak subjects who never returned (r=0). Total returns do not differ by skill (F=0.67).
agent_test: Log immediate vs delayed returns per run; compare high-accuracy runs to low-accuracy runs. Then force 'finish one candidate before moving on' vs 'free jumping' at equal tokens.

claim: On an easy position that is solvable within about 9 plies, search statistics barely separate grandmasters from experts or Masters from weaker players: depth, node count and rate are not reliably different. Move quality differs a lot (G 8.2 vs E 5.2 of 9). Mean depth shows only a small slope of about 0.5 to 0.6 ply per 200 Elo.
schema_part: none (design lesson: do not copy 'deeper search' as the expert trait)
agent_test: Do not rely on depth budget alone as the lever; compare adding depth budget vs adding retrieved prior knowledge at equal tokens.

claim: On hard positions that need 23 to 35 plies (52, 60 and 70 nodes), search depth and nodes scale steeply and linearly with skill (mean depth 13.8, 10.5, 7.4, 2.8 plies for GM, IM, CM, class B; 2.4 plies per 200 Elo; max depth 3.6 plies per 200 Elo). Task difficulty decides whether search differences show. Full text of Campitelli and Gobet (2004) now verified: N=4, one player per level, three positions, and two of the three told to find the unique solution. Connors et al. (2011, 22 players) is still abstract-level, and its abstract stresses search speed, not depth. No larger replication of the depth slope was found.
agent_test: Compare a fixed depth budget with a budget that grows with an estimated difficulty signal (e.g. branch disagreement) at equal total tokens.

claim: Skill carries a large part that search statistics do not explain. After removing mean depth, max depth and nodes, Elo still explains 17.6% of move-quality variance (p<.005). The same four players in the 2004 study also won on 5 s recall, 10 s decisions and practice hours. 63 players evaluate positions after 5 s with skill explaining 44% of the error variance and no speed-accuracy trade-off.
schema_part: memory (retrieval of stored patterns before search)
agent_test: Give the agent a retrieved library of solved cases (memory) before search; compare against same tokens spent on extra search passes.

claim: Whether time pressure hurts strong players through lost search is contested. Kasparov lost only about 100 Elo when his move time was cut to one quarter to one eighth. Chabris and Hearst found blunders rose from 5.02 to 6.85 per 1,000 moves (36.5%) with about 6x less time. Both camps read the same effect sizes in opposite ways. Van Harreveld and Burns point in opposite directions (second-hand or abstract only).
agent_test: Sweep the token budget (1x, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and plot accuracy. A flat curve means retrieval dominates; a steep curve means search matters. Compare scaffold vs plain at each level.

claim: Stronger players are more selective, but the pattern is mixed. Gobet (1998): Masters tried 3.2 base moves vs 6.5 for class A, and spent 1.1 min on the first phase vs 4.2 for class B (non-monotonic). De Groot: grandmasters mentioned more moves and more different first moves per minute than experts. Saariluoma: inverted U in nodes.
agent_test: Vary candidate width (2, 3, 5) at fixed total tokens on hard tasks; check whether the best width depends on difficulty.

claim: The first idea can block a better one (Einstellung). Chess experts who found a familiar five-move mate said they were looking for a shorter one but did not find the three-move mate. IMs scored like class A players, Masters like class B, candidate masters like class C, so about 3 SD of skill was lost. Odds of finding the shorter line fell by a factor 3.67 per 100 Elo lost. Eye tracking showed the gaze stayed on the familiar line squares (F(5,20)=0.6, ns). Same lab for both papers. Gap search: in LLMs, higher reasoning effort already raises resistance to Einstellung traps (mARC: best model 0.751 vs physicians 0.66; 55% vs 36% on items physicians missed), but no study tests a forced second pass that excludes the first answer.
schema_part: G (anti-anchoring) / O (forced restart with new representation)
agent_test: After a first valid answer, run a second pass that must avoid the first answer's key elements, versus a plain 'check again' pass, at equal tokens, on tasks with a shorter or better solution.

claim: Asking a model to re-read and revise its own answer without any outside signal does not reliably help and often hurts. Huang et al.: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; Llama-2 62.0 to 36.5. Kamoi et al. survey: no prior work shows success with feedback from prompted LLMs alone except on unusually suited tasks; external feedback, tools, or fine-tuning make it work. ThinkRetrieve: plain forced-Wait continuation stalled or fell at larger budgets (DeepSeek-R1-1.5B on GSM8K 83% to 52% at 22K tokens). Revisits that add relevant retrieved examples did not fall (see K18).
agent_test: Run intrinsic 'review your answer' passes vs verifier-grounded passes at equal tokens; log right-to-wrong flips.

claim: Revisiting can go wrong in both directions for reasoning models. Wrong answers carry 225% more tokens and 418% more thought switches, and over 70% of wrong answers contain a correct thought (underthinking). A decoding penalty on switch words raised QwQ dev accuracy 35.2 to 39.8. In the opposite direction, forcing 'Wait' continuation lifted s1-32B on AIME24 from 50.0 to 53.3 (2 Waits) and 56.7 (4 Waits), a gain of 1 or 2 problems of 30. Effects are small and from fine-tuned or decode-level interventions.
schema_part: S5 (when to stay vs switch) / G
agent_test: Test three scaffold arms at equal tokens: stay on the current line until a stop test passes, free switching, forced re-check. Measure accuracy and switch count.

claim: Explicit tree search with evaluation, pruning and backtracking beats flat chain of thought at comparable token cost on lookahead tasks. Game of 24: ToT b=5 74% at 5.5k completion tokens vs CoT best-of-100 49% at 6.7k tokens (CoT-SC k=100 9.0% in the main table). Mini crosswords word-level: ToT 60%, no backtracking 20%, no pruning 41.5%. Chess: wrapping a 2.7B model in MCTS added about 68 Elo at 100 simulations (internal Elo, checked) and about 300 Elo at 2000 simulations (as reported, partly unchecked).
agent_test: Same task set, equal tokens: single chain vs best-of-N vs tree with backtrack and prune. Ablate backtrack and prune separately.

claim: General chat LLMs are weak at chess decisions, and thinking helps much. Two-candidate choice: o1-preview 76.6%, claude-3.5-sonnet 54.9% (chance 50). ChessQA: thinking gave +14.7 points on average; GPT-5 79.3% with vs 44.0% without; Short Tactics averaged 17.4%. ChessArena and SPIN-Bench: no LLM beat a weak engine; board-state errors a leading failure.
agent_test: Use chess puzzles with a known best move as one external test domain; compare plain thinking vs scaffold at equal tokens.

claim: Written reasoning branches in LLMs are shallow and weakly tied to the choice. In a four-in-a-row study mean max depth was 1.78 plies (humans 4 to 6 inferred); deleting the chosen move's branch changed the move in 32.0% of cases, while deleting the largest unchosen branch changed it in 1.2%. Chess explanations mostly mirror the chosen move. Not re-checked by this cross-check. Status lowered after the gap search: no replication of the 32.0% vs 1.2% ablation was found; related but different tests are in K19.
schema_part: S4 (make branch evaluation actually drive the choice)
agent_test: Parse the scaffold trace; measure whether removing the deepest unchosen branch changes the final answer. Require the decision to cite the evaluated branches.

claim: Training a model on search traces that contain dead ends and backtracking beats training on the optimal path alone: Countdown 51.27% vs 25.73% (SoS, from-scratch small model); Sokoban optimal 93.7% vs 86.8% (Searchformer). Needs training and a symbolic solver. Not usable by a prompt-only scaffold, except as a hint that messy search is a better exemplar than clean answers.
agent_test: Few-shot exemplars with explored-and-abandoned branches vs clean-solution exemplars at equal prompt tokens.

claim: Returns to a candidate have identifiable triggers: a detected error, a lowered expectancy of other moves, or a need to confirm. Immediate returns mostly clarify; delayed returns serve overall deepening. A position type that needs comparing tried moves (position C) produced the most returns (c 4.2 vs 2.4). In 15% of protocols the move played was not the last one investigated.
agent_test: Add explicit revisit triggers (conflict between branches, low confidence) vs unconditional revisits at equal tokens; log whether final answer equals the last explored.

claim: Trainer advice (Kotov): list candidates, analyse each to one evaluation, never jump between lines. De Groot saw everyone jump. In 2004 two top players (who had read Kotov) were more disciplined; two weaker players jumped without a candidate list. No outcome comparison exists of disciplined vs free search. (2004 full text confirms: the GM jumped but kept a growing candidate list, the IM was the textbook case and had the best move quality by 0.4 points, N=1 each.)
agent_test: A/B: candidate list with finish-each-line vs free jumping at equal tokens.

claim: Recognition and search are interleaved, not rival. SEARCH (Gobet 1997) predicts mean depth as a slow power function of chunks (about 2.5 plies at 1,000 chunks; above 5 plies beyond 100,000) and fits the small slopes in easy positions; it underestimates the steep slope on hard positions. Model claim, not a direct test.
agent_test: Test whether depth gains from a retrieved pattern library follow diminishing returns.

claim: A revisit helps an LLM when it brings new information, and not when it only repeats the check. The best single test is ThinkRetrieve: at the same thinking budget (exemplar tokens counted), plain forced-Wait continuation stalled or fell, random per-step examples helped some, relevant per-step examples helped most, and relevant examples given once up front did little (AIME 2025, Qwen3-1.7B: sequential 22.2, random 27.8, relevant 35.6; wins in every model-benchmark cell). Kamoi et al. reach the same view from the literature: external feedback works, prompt-only feedback mostly does not. The test varies the content of the revisit, but only for retrieved math examples; no study varies verifier vs different sampled path vs different representation.
schema_part: S5 (revisit needs a trigger and a payload) / G
agent_test: At equal tokens, compare four revisit types after a first answer: (a) plain 'check again', (b) a tool or executable check, (c) a fresh independent sample, (d) retrieval of a solved neighbour case. Log right-to-wrong and wrong-to-right flips.

claim: How far the written trace drives the answer depends on the task, and some sentences matter far more than others. Lanham et al.: on three tasks the chain changed the answer under 10% of the time, on AQuA over 60%; larger models relied on it less; filler tokens gave no gain. Thought anchors: planning and uncertainty-management (backtracking) sentences have the highest counterfactual effect on the final answer (R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, 20 MATH problems). Neither test is the branch-removal ablation of K13.
agent_test: Ablate (delete or replace) each branch and each revisit step in the scaffold trace; count how often the final answer changes. Make the final choice a code step over scored candidates, and compare.

claim: Cutting thinking at the best point beats taking the last state, and the loss from overthinking depends on the task. OTBench (six models, 70.5B tokens): on average 64.3% of thinking tokens come after the earliest best prefix and full thinking is 9.03 points below it (MATH 1.83, AIME 4.88, LCB 12.42, GPQA 16.98). Oracle stopping matches full-thinking accuracy at 14.2% of the budget (fixed cap 35.0%). DEER: a confidence test on a trial answer at step transitions cut length 19.1% to 80.1% and changed accuracy by +0.3 to +5.0 points over 11 models. Both papers are from one lab, and the oracle numbers are biased upward by choosing the best prefix on the same probes.
agent_test: At each branch boundary ask for a trial answer with a confidence; stop when it is high and stable, otherwise continue. Compare with always-last answer and fixed budget at equal tokens, per task type.

claim: Spending more tokens on harder items and fewer on easy ones beats uniform spending, and a cheap difficulty signal exists. Snell et al.: difficulty-adaptive choice of strategy matched best-of-N with up to 4x less compute (estimate cost not counted). Nguyen et al.: 4 first samples and their disagreement as the signal gave +2.3% on average over uniform allocation (14 of 15 settings better), up to +5.5%. SelfBudgeter (trained) cut length 61% on math but its 7B model fell on AIME2025 (6.67 vs 28.89), so budget prediction can fail on the hardest items.
agent_test: Run 3 to 4 cheap first passes, use answer disagreement to set the budget for the rest, with a floor for items that look hard. Compare with a uniform split at the same total tokens.

claim: Whether to deepen the same line or restart depends on the task. Snell et al.: with a fine-tuned revision model, sequential revisions narrowly beat parallel samples at the same generation count; easy items did best fully sequential, hard items best with a mix. Mirtaheri et al.: on synthetic graph-connectivity tasks built to need serial depth, one long chain beats many short voted chains at a fixed token budget. Chen et al.: iterative deepening with a growing budget and a check trigger beat vanilla sampling at equal wall-clock (AIME-24 pass@1 72.6 vs 75.5, cons@32 83.3 vs 86.7; 30 problems). Snell's revision model needed fine-tuning, so these do not directly decide a prompt-only rule.
schema_part: S4/S5 (stay on a line vs restart)
agent_test: At equal tokens on tasks of known difficulty, compare: deepen the first line, restart from scratch with an excluded-first-answer rule, and a 50/50 mix. Report by difficulty tier.

claim: A library of solved cases can beat extra sampling at a matched sampling budget, but the matching is not exact in tokens. Reasoning Memory (32M procedural entries): 0.580 vs 0.500 average for no retrieval, +8.9% over a compute-matched retrieval-free baseline at the higher budget, 34 of 36 wins over that baseline. ThinkRetrieve counts exemplar tokens against the budget and still wins. Document and full-trajectory retrieval mostly did not help. Two 2026 preprints from different groups, neither replicated.
schema_part: memory (retrieval of stored cases before and during search)
agent_test: Equal total tokens (retrieved text included): memory-of-solved-cases arm vs extra-search arm vs both, on held-out tasks, and with the memory emptied as a control.
